title: Going From Tower Defense To 3D Platformer Made Me Respect Jump Physics A Lot More
author: Top-Cardiologist1011
selftext:
I previously built a small 3D tower defense game, so I thought a short 3D platformer would be only a little harder.

That was very wrong.

Game context: [https://games.xgallery.online/forest-quest/](https://games.xgallery.online/forest-quest/)

Tower defense had a lot of systems, but almost no real-time physical feel. Enemies followed paths, towers fired, UI updated. If a number was off, I could tune damage or speed.

Forest Quest is also small, only 6 levels, but the player can feel bad physics in about two seconds.

The current jump setup is:

Jump velocity: 10

Double jump velocity: 8

Gravity: 25

Run multiplier: 1.6

Stomp bounce: 8

Those numbers look random, but they came from trying to make one jump clear about a 1.5m gap without feeling floaty. Too much gravity made the fox drop like a brick. Too little made every platform feel like low gravity.

The camera was another rabbit hole. I ended up with a follow lerp around 0.1. At 0.3 it felt twitchy when jumping. At 0.05 the fox could run toward the edge of the screen before the camera caught up.

The part that surprised me most was moving platforms. If the player stands on a platform, jumps, and the platform keeps moving, should the player inherit that sideways motion? The answer is yes, or it feels like the platform slips out from under you.

I used simple AABB collision and downward raycasts instead of a physics engine, mostly because I wanted direct control. It was less code than expected, but way more tuning than expected.

The 3D models were the easy part this time. I used Meshy for the fox, mushroom, sprite, golem, boss, and props, so the hard part moved from "how do I model this" to "why does this jump feel slightly wrong."

Platformers are cruel in a good way. They expose every lazy assumption in your movement code.
